title: Judah's Family Tree Leading to David
overview: This chapter traces the tribe of Judah from its founder down through many clans, giving special attention to the line that produced King David.

parts.label: Israel's twelve sons (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The twelve sons of Jacob, also called Israel, are the ancestors of Israel's twelve tribes. The writer names them all but turns first to Judah, because Israel's royal family of David came from that tribe.

parts.label: Judah's troubled beginnings (vv. 3-8)
parts.note: The list keeps the family's failures in view: Er's death, Judah's sons by his daughter-in-law Tamar (Genesis 38), and Achan, who kept plunder from Jericho that was meant to be given wholly to God (Joshua 7). Here his name is spelled Achar, likely a play on the Hebrew word for "trouble," while other descendants of Zerah are remembered as famously wise men.

parts.label: The line to King David (vv. 9-17)
parts.note: This chain runs through Nahshon, a tribal leader in the wilderness, and Boaz from the book of Ruth, to Jesse's son David, listed as seventh even though 1 Samuel mentions eight sons, perhaps because one died young. Christians later read this line as the ancestry of Jesus, as Matthew's family list does.

parts.label: Hezron's wider family (vv. 18-24)
parts.note: Caleb's line includes Bezalel, the craftsman who built Israel's portable worship tent in the time of Moses. Hezron's late marriage into a family east of the Jordan explains why his descendant Jair held towns there, some later lost to neighboring peoples, though the Hebrew of verse 24 is unclear and scholars are unsure what it says.

parts.label: Jerahmeel and an Egyptian heir (vv. 25-41)
parts.note: The record quietly notes men who died without children, and Sheshan, who had only daughters. He married one daughter to his Egyptian servant Jarha, and the family line continued through that foreigner for many generations.

parts.label: Caleb's clans and towns (vv. 42-55)
parts.note: Here "father of" a town, such as Bethlehem or Hebron, usually means its founder or leading clan, so this part works like a map of who settled where in Judah. It ends with Kenites, a non-Israelite people who lived among Judah, including families of scribes linked to the Rechabites.

think: This family record keeps the failures, the childless and the outsiders right alongside the famous names; what do you think a family gains or loses by telling its story that way?
